flashcards.q: What are the three families of feature selection and their core tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Filter (score vs target, no model, cheap, misses interactions) · Wrapper (RFE, model performance as score, expensive O(p) to O(p^2) retrains, most accurate for that model) · Embedded (L1, tree importance; selection is a byproduct of one training run, interaction-aware, inherits model bias).

flashcards.q: Why is tree-based feature_importances_ (Gini/MDI) biased toward high-cardinality features?
flashcards.a: CART evaluates every candidate threshold on every feature at each split. A high-cardinality/continuous feature offers far more candidate thresholds than a binary one, so by chance it's more likely to produce a locally good split -- a multiple-comparisons effect. Strobl et al. (2007) showed a random 20-category feature outranking a genuinely predictive binary one in simulation.

flashcards.q: Does SHAP fix the cardinality bias that afflicts Gini importance?
flashcards.a: Partially. SHAP fixes the axioms (local accuracy, consistency) that Gini importance lacks, but TreeExplainer still inherits a milder version of the same high-cardinality bias when the underlying tree structure it's explaining is itself biased.

flashcards.q: What is the feature-selection CV leakage bug and how do you fix it?
flashcards.a: Fitting a selector (e.g. SelectKBest) on the full dataset before train/test split lets selection see labels from rows that end up in the 'held-out' set, inflating CV scores. Fix: put selection inside a sklearn Pipeline so it refits fresh inside each CV fold.

flashcards.q: How bad can feature-selection leakage get, numerically?
flashcards.a: Selecting the top 20 of 10,000 candidate columns on only 500 rows can produce a CV AUC above 0.85 on pure noise -- with that many candidates, some correlate with the label by chance, and selection systematically harvests that chance correlation.

flashcards.q: Would a filter method (correlation, chi2, mutual info) catch y = X1 XOR X2 where each feature is individually uncorrelated with y?
flashcards.a: No. Filter methods score each feature against the target in isolation and both X1 and X2 have ~zero marginal correlation, so both get discarded regardless of threshold. Only a model or method that considers the pair jointly (a tree, a wrapper) recovers the signal.

flashcards.q: How does permutation importance work and where does it mislead you?
flashcards.a: Shuffle one column on HELD-OUT data, measure the drop in a real metric -- model-agnostic, immune to Gini's split-count bias. It misleads under correlated features: shuffling one of two highly correlated columns barely hurts the score because the model still has the redundant other one, so both score as unimportant even though the pair matters.

flashcards.q: Why does L1 (Lasso) zero out coefficients exactly while L2 (Ridge) doesn't?
flashcards.a: L1's penalty |w| has a non-differentiable corner at zero, and the L1 constraint region has corners on the axes, so the optimum often lands exactly at zero. L2's penalty w^2 is smooth with a spherical constraint region -- it shrinks coefficients toward zero but essentially never reaches it exactly.

flashcards.q: Why does L1-based feature selection require scaled features?
flashcards.a: The L1 penalty applies to raw coefficient magnitude. An unscaled feature measured in the thousands gets penalized far more per unit of predictive contribution than one measured in single digits, biasing selection toward large-scale features for reasons unrelated to predictive value.

flashcards.q: State the curse of dimensionality with an actual number.
flashcards.a: To match the sample density of N points in 1D, you need N^d points in d dimensions. With N=100 and d=10, that's 10^20 points. Distance/density-based methods (kNN, LOF) degrade sharply from this; tree ensembles degrade more gracefully.

flashcards.q: What is the retrain cost of RFECV on 200 features with step=1 and 5-fold CV, and how do you cut it?
flashcards.a: Roughly 200 x 5 = 1000 full model fits before convergence. Use step=0.1 (drop 10% of remaining features per round) to trade ranking granularity for a large speedup, or switch to embedded selection which trains once.

flashcards.q: sklearn's mutual_info_classif default n_neighbors -- what does it control and what's the risk of leaving it default?
flashcards.a: Default n_neighbors=3, controlling the k-NN density estimator used to estimate mutual information for continuous features. A small k produces noisier, higher-variance MI estimates on small samples.

flashcards.q: A SHAP summary plot ranks a customer_id_hash-derived feature near the top of global importance. What's your first move?
flashcards.a: Investigate before trusting it -- a near-identifier ranking high is the textbook symptom of cardinality bias carrying through into SHAP, or of target leakage. Drop clearly identifier-like columns before training regardless of ranking, and check for leakage on any surprising top feature.

flashcards.q: XGBoost feature_importances_ default type ('weight' vs 'gain' vs 'cover') -- which inherits the cardinality bias hardest and why?
flashcards.a: 'weight' (split count) inherits it hardest since it's literally a count of times split on, directly rewarding features with more candidate thresholds. 'gain' (average loss reduction) is somewhat more robust but not immune -- a spurious split on a high-cardinality noise feature that reduces loss slightly still counts toward gain.
